title: Maslow's Pyramid
objective: After this level you can explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs and what later research changed about it.
summary: Maslow's 1943 hierarchy ranks needs from food to self-actualization. He never drew the pyramid, said the order isn't rigid, and a 123-country study backs that up.

cards.headline: It's in almost every textbook. Maslow never drew it.
cards.body: Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs usually appears as a pyramid, with food at the bottom and fulfillment at the top. The needs are his. The pyramid, and the strict one-floor-at-a-time climb it suggests, came from someone else.

cards.headline: Five kinds of need
cards.body: In a 1943 paper, Maslow proposed a ladder of needs: physiological needs like food, then safety, love and belonging, esteem, and at the top self-actualization, which he called the desire to become everything one is capable of becoming. Lower needs generally come first. If you're struggling to find enough to eat, you're unlikely to worry much about how others see you.

cards.headline: Who built the pyramid?
cards.body: In 2019, Todd Bridgman and colleagues went looking for Maslow's pyramid and found he never drew one. They traced it to a 1960 article by Charles McDermid, a consulting psychologist. Maslow himself had warned, in that same 1943 paper, that his order was "not nearly as rigid" as it might sound; most people have every need only partly met at once.

cards.headline: What the world data say
cards.body: Then the idea met real numbers. In 2011, Louis Tay and Ed Diener looked at 123 countries. Meeting each need was linked to wellbeing largely regardless of whether other needs were met. Social needs mattered even where safety needs were unmet. The ladder turns out to be more of a web.

cards.headline: Maslow: reconsidered
learned: Maslow ranked needs from food to self-actualization
He never drew the pyramid; McDermid did in 1960
He said the order is not rigid
In 123 countries, needs mattered largely independently

questions.prompt: Maslow put _____ at the top of his 1943 hierarchy of needs.

options.label: esteem
options.rationale: Esteem sits just below the top.

options.label: safety
options.rationale: Safety is near the bottom, after physiological needs.

questions.explanation: Self-actualization, becoming everything one is capable of becoming, sits at the top of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Why is the famous pyramid a misleading picture of what Maslow proposed?

options.label: Maslow drew it upside down in his 1943 paper
options.rationale: He never drew a pyramid at all.

options.label: He said the order was not rigid, and never drew it
He put self-actualization at the bottom
options.rationale: It was at the top of his list.

options.label: He listed only two needs, not five
options.rationale: He listed five kinds of need.

questions.explanation: Maslow never drew a pyramid (Charles McDermid did, in 1960), and he wrote that the order is "not nearly as rigid" as it might sound.

questions.prompt: Maslow's lowest level holds needs like food. Which Level 41 idea explains how hunger gets you moving?

options.label: Incentives pulling you toward rewards
options.rationale: Incentives pull from outside; hunger comes from inside.

options.label: Self-actualization at the top of the ladder
options.rationale: That is the highest need, not the lowest.

options.label: Drive theory: a slip from balance creates a drive
The overjustification of a habit
options.rationale: That term is about rewards and interest, not hunger.

questions.explanation: Physiological needs work like Level 41's drives: when blood sugar drops, homeostasis slips and hunger pushes you to eat.
